title: Want to Use AI to Improve Your Work? Have It Disagree with You - Nautilus
gist: Truncated teaser by researcher Monideepa Tarafdar: generative AI use by knowledge workers risks cognitive offloading and low-quality answers, but her interview study of 45 university knowledge workers suggests prompting AI to disagree with you can instead raise novel solutions.

insights.claim: Recent research shows people who use generative AI for work tasks can stop thinking critically and surrender to the AI's quick, confident answers, producing fast but low-quality solutions.
insights.speaker: Monideepa Tarafdar
insights.so_what: Productivity gains from gen-AI adoption may be overstated if output quality degrades; watch for quality metrics, not just speed.
insights.quote: They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

insights.claim: Scholars call this increasingly prevalent problem cognitive offloading and are finding it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.
insights.speaker: Monideepa Tarafdar
insights.so_what: Long-run human-capital erosion is a hidden cost of AI deployment for firms dependent on expert judgment.
insights.quote: it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable

insights.claim: Prompting a generative AI model to fight against the user's point of view can surface novel solutions rather than inducing passive acceptance.
insights.speaker: Monideepa Tarafdar
insights.so_what: Product design that builds in AI disagreement or critique modes may differentiate enterprise AI tools.
insights.locator: Prompting an AI model to fight

insights.claim: Tarafdar and colleagues interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university who used generative AI for ideation, complex problem-solving and solution design, and analyzed their iterative prompts and outputs.
insights.speaker: Monideepa Tarafdar
insights.so_what: Small qualitative sample; treat the remedy as a hypothesis pending larger studies.
insights.quote: my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university
